chapters.name: Chapter 1: Reconnecting with family and children

lessons.title: Lesson 1: Planning your first contact
lessons.text:
Lesson 1 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Choose who to contact first and write a short, respectful first message.
This lesson builds toward: Given the people you want to reconnect with, you will choose who to contact first and write a short, respectful first message, with no demand for money, blame or pressure, and following any court order.
While you were away, your family kept living. Children grew, people moved, some relationships got stronger and some got hurt. Reconnecting goes best when you plan it instead of showing up unannounced.
Start by making a list of the people you want back in your life. Next to each name, write how things were left and whether there is any court order, such as a no-contact or custody order. Follow every order. If you are not sure, ask your parole or probation officer or legal aid.
Pick one person who is likely to be open, and start small: a letter, a text or a short call. Say you are home, say you would like to reconnect, and let them choose the pace. Do not ask for money or a place to stay in the first message.
Expect mixed feelings, including your own. If someone is not ready, thank them and leave the door open. That is not the end; it is the start.
Step by step:
- List the people you want to reconnect with.
- Note how things were left and any court orders; follow every order.
- Choose one person likely to be open.
- Write a short message: you are home, you would like to reconnect, they can choose the pace.
- Send it, then give them time to answer.
Words to know:
- No-contact order: a court order that says you may not contact a certain person.
- Custody order: a court order about who children live with and who makes decisions for them.
- Pace: how fast something happens.
Try it now: Write your list of people, then choose one person and write a first message of three or four sentences. Read it out loud. Take out anything that asks for money, blames anyone or pushes for a quick answer.
You can now plan a first contact, follow any court orders, and write a short, respectful message that lets the other person choose the pace.

check.q: What should a first message to a family member include?
options: A request to stay at their place
That you are home and would like to reconnect
A list of what they did wrong
A demand for an answer today
check.why: A short, respectful message opens the door without pressure.

check.q: Your brother replies that he needs time before talking. What would you do?
options: Call him every day until he answers
Thank him and leave the door open
Ask other family to pressure him
check.why: Respecting his pace keeps the door open for later.

lessons.title: Lesson 2: Reconnecting with your children
lessons.text:
Lesson 2 of 6 · about 6 minutes
Goal: Plan a first visit or call with your child that puts the child's needs first.
This lesson builds toward: Given a child you want to reconnect with, you will plan a first visit or call that puts the child's needs first, with questions for the caregiver and one small promise you can keep.
Children need three things from a returning parent: safety, honesty they can understand, and a parent who shows up again and again. Being consistent matters more than big gifts or big promises.
Work with the adult who cares for your child now. Ask them what the child knows, what the child is ready for, and what times work. Speak respectfully about the other parent or caregiver in front of the child, even when it is hard.
Be honest in words that fit the child's age. A young child may only need: I made a mistake, I was away, and I am here now. Older children may have questions or anger. Listen, do not argue, and do not make promises you cannot keep.
If you need visits or a change in custody, your state court's self-help website explains the forms, and family law facilitators or legal aid can help. Never take a child or pressure a caregiver outside a court order.
Step by step:
- Talk with the child's caregiver first.
- Ask what the child knows and is ready for.
- Plan a short first visit or call at a time that works for the child.
- Use honest words that fit the child's age.
- Keep every promise, starting with small ones, such as calling when you said you would.
Words to know:
- Caregiver: the adult who looks after a child day to day.
- Visitation: the time a parent spends with a child who does not live with them, often set by a court.
- Family law facilitator: a court helper who explains family law forms, often for free.
Try it now: Write down three questions to ask your child's caregiver before a first visit or call, and one small promise you know you can keep, such as calling every Sunday at 6 pm.
You can now plan a first visit or call that puts your child first, work with the caregiver, and keep small promises that build trust.

check.q: What builds a child's trust most after a parent comes home?
options: Keeping small promises again and again
check.why: Children trust a parent who keeps showing up and keeping small promises.

check.q: You want to call your daughter for the first time in years. What would you do first?
check.why: The caregiver can help plan contact that puts the child's needs first.

lessons.title: Lesson 3: Child support: asking for a review
lessons.text:
Lesson 3 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Ask your child support agency for a review when your order no longer fits your income.
This lesson builds toward: Given a child support order that no longer fits your income, you will ask your child support agency for a review, with the agency's contact, the papers needed and a date to contact them.
Child support does not stop by itself when your income changes. Unpaid support can build up into a large debt and lead to things like a suspended driver's license. Ignoring it makes it worse. Asking for a review is the right move.
In California, either parent can ask the local child support agency for a review and adjustment, called a modification. There is no charge. It can apply when the order would change by 20% or $50, whichever is less. Changes that count include losing or starting a job, a change in income, custody changes, disability, incarceration and military deployment. A parent who will be incarcerated for 60 days or more in a row can ask for a lower order using the Incarcerated Parent's Request to Review Child Support form.
Bring proof of your income and expenses, such as pay stubs or a benefits letter. If both parents agree, they can sign an agreement for the court; if not, the court decides. Your county's family law facilitator can help.
Outside California, contact your state or tribal child support agency and ask how to request a review. Ask early: in many places a change only counts from the date you ask, not from when your income dropped.
Step by step:
- Find your local child support agency (in California, childsupport.ca.gov).
- Call or write to ask for a review and adjustment.
- Gather proof of income and expenses.
- Keep copies and write down the date you asked.
- Pay what you can while you wait, and keep records of every payment.
Words to know:
- Child support order: a court order saying how much a parent pays to help support a child.
- Modification: a change to a child support order.
- Arrears: child support that was owed and not paid.
Official sources:
- California Department of Child Support Services: Modify my payment
- California Department of Child Support Services: Home
Try it now: Find your child support agency's website or phone number. Write down how to ask for a review, the papers they want, and the date you will contact them. If you have no order, write down one way you can help your child this month.
You can now ask your child support agency for a review and bring the right proof, instead of letting unpaid support build up.

check.q: What can happen if you ignore child support after your income drops?
options: Unpaid support can build into a large debt
The child support agency forgets about it
check.why: Ignored support keeps adding up, so asking for a review matters.

check.q: You lost hours at work and your child support order is now too high. What would you do?
options: Ask a friend to call for you
Contact your child support agency and ask for a review
check.why: A review is the official way to match an order to your income.

lessons.title: Lesson 4: Listening, apologizing and rebuilding trust
lessons.text:
Lesson 4 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Use listening, I-statements and a real apology in a hard conversation.
This lesson builds toward: Given a hard conversation, you will use listening, I-statements and a three-part apology, with no "but" in the apology and no request to be forgiven.
Trust is rebuilt by actions over time, not in one talk. Good communication helps those actions be seen.
Listen first. Let the other person finish, then say back what you heard: So you felt let down when I missed your graduation. This shows you understand, even if you see it differently.
Use I-statements to share your feelings without blaming: I feel nervous about this, instead of You always make this hard. A real apology names what you did, says how it hurt them, and says what you will do differently. It does not include but, and it does not demand forgiveness.
Some people will need a long time. Be patient. Keep showing up, keep your word, and let the trust come back at their speed.
Step by step:
- Let the other person finish talking.
- Say back what you heard.
- Share your feelings with I-statements.
- Apologize: what you did, how it hurt, what you will do differently.
- Do not add but; do not demand forgiveness.
- Keep your word afterward.
Words to know:
- I-statement: a way to share your feelings starting with I, without blaming.
- Reflect back: repeating in your own words what someone said, to show you understood.
- Trust: believing someone will do what they say.
Try it now: Write a real apology to one person, using the three parts: what you did, how it hurt them, and what you will do differently. Check it has no but and does not ask to be forgiven. You decide later whether and when to share it.
You can now listen and reflect back, speak with I-statements, and give a real apology that helps rebuild trust.

check.q: What are the three parts of a real apology?
options: What you did, how it hurt them, and what you will do differently
Why you did it, who else was at fault, and what they should do
Sorry, but, and please forgive me
A gift, a hug and a promise to forget
check.why: A real apology names the harm and the change without excuses.

check.q: Your mother starts telling you how hurt she felt. What would you do first?
check.why: Listening first shows respect and helps rebuild trust.

lessons.title: Lesson 5: Mentors, faith and community groups
lessons.text:
Lesson 5 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Find a mentor and one community group you can join this month.
This lesson builds toward: Using 211, your case manager or local groups, you will find a mentor and one community group and ask the mentor for a specific commitment, with contact details for each and the exact words of your ask.
A mentor is someone a few steps ahead of you who can give advice, check in and cheer you on. Many reentry programs match people with mentors, often people who have come home themselves.
Community groups give you a place to belong: reentry support groups, recovery meetings, faith communities, sports leagues, volunteer groups, parenting classes and alumni groups from programs you finished. Being around people who are building good lives makes it easier to do the same.
To find them, ask your reentry program, case manager or parole officer, call 211, or ask a faith community near you. Go once, then go again. Most groups feel strange at first and better by the third visit.
When you ask someone to be a mentor, be specific: Could we talk for 30 minutes once a month? I am working on keeping my job and reconnecting with my kids.
Step by step:
- Ask your reentry program or case manager about mentors.
- Call 211 or ask a faith community about groups near you.
- Pick one group and go at least three times.
- Ask a possible mentor for a specific, small commitment.
- Thank people who help you.
Words to know:
- Mentor: a trusted person who gives advice and support as you grow.
- Support group: people with a shared experience who meet to help each other.
- Faith community: a church, mosque, temple or other place of worship and its members.
Official sources:
- 211: Find local help
Try it now: Find one possible mentor and one community group. Write down how to reach each. Then write the exact words you will use to ask the mentor for a small, specific commitment.
You can now find a mentor and a community group and ask for support in a clear, specific way.

options: A trusted person a few steps ahead who gives advice and support
check.why: A mentor has walked a similar road and helps guide you.

check.q: You want someone at your church to mentor you. What would you say?
options: Can you be there for me whenever I need you?
Could we meet for 30 minutes once a month about my goals?
check.why: A small, specific ask is easier for a mentor to say yes to.

lessons.title: Lesson 6: Healthy boundaries and getting support
lessons.text:
Lesson 6 of 6 · about 6 minutes
Goal: Set two healthy boundaries and build a support list that includes 988.
This lesson builds toward: Given people or situations that could set you back, you will set two healthy boundaries and write a support list that includes 988, with the list kept in your phone and on paper.
A boundary is a line you draw to protect your health, your freedom and your progress. Some old friends, places and habits can pull you back. A boundary might be: I do not go to that block anymore, or I will not keep anything in my car for anyone.
Say a boundary simply and kindly: I care about you, and I cannot be around drinking right now. You do not need to argue or explain it many times. Boundaries also go both ways: respect the boundaries your family sets with you.
Coming home is stressful. Feeling anxious, angry, sad or alone is common, and help is normal. The 988 Suicide and Crisis Lifeline is free, confidential and open 24 hours a day, every day. You can call or text 988, or chat at 988lifeline.org, for yourself or someone you are worried about. In an emergency, call 911.
Make a support list: two or three people you trust, your mentor or group, your case manager, and 988. Keep it in your phone and on paper.
Step by step:
- Name two situations that could pull you back.
- Write a boundary for each.
- Practice saying each one kindly and simply.
- Write your support list: trusted people, mentor or group, case manager, 988.
- Keep the list in your phone and on paper.
Words to know:
- Boundary: a limit you set to protect your health, safety and progress.
- 988: the Suicide and Crisis Lifeline; call, text or chat for free, 24/7.
- Trigger: a person, place or feeling that makes an old habit feel stronger.
Official sources:
- 988 Suicide and Crisis Lifeline
Try it now: Final task: write your one-page reconnection and support plan with the first family member you will contact and your message, one parenting or child support step if it applies, two community supports, two boundaries, and your support list with 988 on it.
You can now set healthy boundaries, say them kindly, and reach for support, including 988, when things get hard.
How your final task is checked:
What we look at Not yet Meets Exceeds First contact No message, or it asks for money, blames or pushes. Names who to contact first and a short, respectful message. The message was read out loud and leaves room for the person to take their time. Parenting or child support step No step when one applies. One clear step, such as contacting the caregiver or asking the agency for a review, with a date. Lists the papers needed or the questions for the caregiver. Community supports Fewer than two supports. Two supports, such as a mentor, group or faith community, with how to reach them. Includes the exact words to ask a mentor for a specific commitment. Boundaries Fewer than two boundaries, or they are vague. Two clear boundaries that protect the learner's progress. Each boundary has the words the learner will use to keep it. Support list No list, or 988 is missing. A list of people and numbers to call, including 988. Saved in the phone and on paper. To pass: Meets or Exceeds on every row. If a row is Not yet, fix that part and try again.

options: A limit you set to protect your health and progress
A rule your family sets for you
check.why: Boundaries are limits you choose to protect yourself and your progress.

check.q: An old friend keeps inviting you to places that could get you in trouble. What would you do?
options: Go once so they stop asking
Kindly say no and suggest something else, or step back
check.why: A clear, kind no protects your progress.
